mr. president, self-employment is an effective method of combating rising unemployment. however, regardless of all the positive effects of this method, it is of the utmost importance that this form of employment enjoys a high level of social protection, such as the exercise of social rights based on maternity and paternity, pension and health insurance. member states should therefore encourage unemployed workers to self-employ by strengthening the social elements of this employment instrument and by providing the same level of protection as that enjoyed by employees in the private and public sectors. it would also be advisable to reduce the social benefits of self-employed workers for a limited period of time in order to relieve them of the burden of self-employment. in doing so, the risk of the possibility of false self-employment and potential abuse in this part of the exercise of social rights should be reduced. quality and comprehensive labour and social legislation are prerequisites for economic growth and development throughout the union.

mr president, consumers in a consumer society can be defined as the largest group of people who live under false assumptions: from the false assumption that they eat healthy food to the one that they buy products manufacturered in an environmentally-acceptable manner and humane manufacturing conditions. one of the most frequently encountered false assumptions in europe is that under the same brand name we always buy the same product. this is simply not so. despite high standards prescribed by the eu, products launched on the markets of developed countries, where they are of high quality, are sold under the same brand on the markets of new member states, and especially on the markets of accession countries, but the quality is often not the same. this is true for a range of products, from food and clothes to technical products. the practice should be stopped, as it serves only to help the rich become richer and destroys what is left of domestic production.

written. - i voted in favour of the report because i believe there is irrefutable evidence that the italian mep, lara comi, in the controversial programme of last january, made her speech as a representative of this high body of the union, and not as a member of a national party. since article 8 of the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european union, to which lara comi refers expressly in her request for protection, provides that members of the european parliament may not be subject to any form of investigation, detention or judicial proceedings for expressing opinions or voting in the performance of their duties, i consider it appropriate to protect the immunity of ms comi.

written. − i have supported this proposal for an amendment to the voting rules and the content of the report on the european parliament's consent procedure. one of the significant changes is the explicit clarification and suggestion that the plenary vote on giving consent rather than on the recommendations of the competent rapporteur of the parliamentary committee, as there have been cases where the practice of voting on a recommendation has led to confusion. thus, irrespective of the recommendation of the competent parliamentary committee, parliament votes on whether or not to give its consent. such clarifications of the voting rules are important to reduce the possibility of double interpretation in the future.
written. - this is a very high-quality report, which refers to rule 81 of the rules of procedure of the european parliament on the consent procedure, more specifically to the shortcomings of that rule, which in practice are manifested by the frequent abuse of the consent procedure. the abuse is that political statements and recommendations are added to the committee procedure and voted on separately from the procedure itself, which in practice leads to a number of complications as parliament's consent must be given by a positive act, not by an act expressly contradicting a recommendation. by recommending that no recitals be allowed in the consent procedure, but that the committee responsible be allowed to accompany its recommendation in plenary by a non-legislative resolution, the rapporteur has struck an excellent balance between the legislative and pragmatic role of parliament in the procedure. that's why i voted yes.
mr president, i support the report by mr krahmer on the regulation to determine ways of achieving the 2020 target of reducing co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles. these vehicles emit 13,5% of the total co2 emissions in the european union and the proposals made contribute to the achievement of the set greenhouse gas reduction targets of 60% by 2050 and 2020 respectively. we had in croatia in 2008 133 500 light commercial vehicles, and last year there were just over 5 000 newly registered. the energy efficiency report for trucks and light commercial vehicles shows a significant increase in energy efficiency in that sector. the report sets long-term targets for 2020 of 147 g co2 emissions, which will ensure environmental objectives and stability for companies that need time to develop new technologies. i also think it's a very good system of so-called super credits for the production of vehicles with extremely low emissions below 50 g co2.
written. − environmental protection is one of the broadest areas of the eu2020 strategy. it is necessary to set the guidelines early enough that will lead us in the future to the desired progress. the eu2020 joint strategy of all member states sets a clear target of reducing co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles to 147 g/km by 2020. more ambitious co2 reduction targets are feasible, but it is important to steer manufacturers in the right direction to encourage investment in green technologies without compromising competitiveness. i would also like to look at the positive example of croatia. the commission notes that the tax exemption for the use of electric cars is not a tax exemption for the use of electric cars. the environmental tax is calculated on the basis of the purchase value of the vehicle and the co2 emissions, which means that cars emitting less than 120 grams of co2 per kilometre are cheaper, those emitting between 120 and 130 grams per kilometre remain at the same or slightly lower price, and those with co2 emissions above 130 grams per kilometre are significantly more expensive. in conclusion, i would like to point out that setting co2 reduction targets encourages european car manufacturers to innovate technologically, thus not only improving the economy but also saving the environment. this regulation improves the quality of life of citizens, but also gives the automotive industry an incentive to look for new ways to reduce emissions.

written. − employee financial participation in companies' revenues is one of the ways of involving and motivating employees, fostering a sense of ownership and reinforcing mutual respect between employers and employees. the three main employee financial participation models that a company can choose are: revenue sharing (cash, deferred or in shares), share ownership for individual employees (employee shares or stock options) and employee stock ownership schemes. although the eu recognises the usefulness of employee financial participation schemes, this is not an area of eu competence and this report is a recommendation to member states. the eu could provide an outline concept with general guidelines on basic principles and best practice to assist in the decision-making on employee financial participation schemes at national and company level. there are a number of measures that could be taken at eu level to facilitate the implementation of employee financial participation schemes in the member states, ranging from the prevention of double taxation to concrete frameworks for action built on the success stories of other member states. employee financial participation is a mechanism that contributes to the europe 2020 core objectives of smart, sustainable and inclusive growth by increasing the involvement of workers in decision-making in the companies in which they work, encouraging the strengthening of good governance and ensuring a share of the financial benefits of successful business operations, and i therefore support this report.

written. − i welcome the efforts of the rapporteur to bridge the gap between opponents and supporters of the commission's 2012 proposal on restricting access to the eu public procurement market by third countries. i consider the rapporteur's note to be of high quality, suggesting that the commission closely monitor the impact of the regulation once it has entered into force and amend it accordingly. i agree with the finding that national and regional provisions vary in different member states and that in order to prevent distortions of the internal market, it should be made clear that member states or their contracting authorities may not restrict access to goods and services from third countries in any way other than as set out in this regulation. however, i believe that the implementation of the commission's proposal in practice could potentially have far-reaching negative consequences on market access and harm the market's growth potential. so i abstained in the vote.
mr. president, honey as a food product has a distinctive production cycle. each of the production steps in that chain must be clearly regulated so that the final consumer is aware of the characteristics of the final product. regardless of whether we define pollen as an ingredient of honey or otherwise, it is of the utmost importance to give the final consumer the possibility to choose by clearly indicating the presence of gmo ingredients if the honey-bearing hives have been grazing in the gmo field. clear national control of such producers allows the boundaries of the gmo field to be clearly defined and the origin of the honey, i.e. the possibility of the presence of a gmo substance in such a product, to be controlled in a logistically simple and at the same time reliable way.
mr. president, citizens have a right to know what they are consuming and in that sense the european court of justice in the bablok case says that honey containing pollen from genetically modified substances needs special marketing authorization. the commission has also concluded that the use of gmos in honey is not a justified and proportionate measure to address the concerns of the union industry. i cannot support this for the sake of the 12 000 beekeepers in croatia, but also for the sake of those across the european union, because the result of such a directive would be the beginning of the end for them. there are between 10 000 and 12 000 beekeepers in croatia and in the last fifteen years the number of hives has increased from 150 000 to 550 000, and croatia now exports some 2 000 tonnes of honey. we want to keep it that way, and if a product contains genetically modified ingredients, consumers need to know about it.
written. − i agree with the views of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety on the status of honeydew, which is following the decision of the european court of justice in case c-442/09, where honeydew is defined as an ingredient of honey. this means that the ingredients found in the honey should be listed, which includes the appearance of honeydew that comes from gm plants. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a list of products authorised to be placed on the market in the union. the interests of european beekeepers, who are mainly small and medium-sized enterprises whose production is increasing, and not only those of the gmo industry, need to be protected. particular support should be given to countries with a clean and unpolluted environment, such as croatia, whose honey is of high quality and whose production of honey has been steadily increasing, in the case of croatia by about 400% over the last 10 years, i.e. from 2 to 7-8 thousand tons of honey. about 2,000 tons of honey are exported, mostly to the european union market. it is the duty of parliament to protect the right of our citizens to know what is in a product, not to circumvent legal norms and in some way deceive the citizens. at the same time, citizens should have the right to choose between products containing and not containing gmos. we can't restrict them.
written. - in the context of the debate on the girling report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending council directive 2001/110/ec on honey, i took account of the arguments put forward by the shadow rapporteur, mr peterle, in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety. the key issue is that pollen of gmo origin is classified as an additive to honey and as such is subject to the legal regulation on the labelling of additives. the court of justice of the european union's decision treating gmo pollen as an additive to honey protects honey producers as well as the right of consumers to be informed about gmo ingredients in food. the european commission proposal and the girling report go in the direction of not requiring industry and resellers of honey to report on the gmo additive in honey. such a scenario is most damaging to small producers, as most of them are in my country. in croatia, according to the croatian beekeeping federation, there are 12,000 honey producers. most of them are small producers who produce honey without gmo pollen. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented in a way that is compatible with the common market.
written. - there are between 10 and 12 thousand beekeepers in croatia. in the last fifteen years, the number of hives has increased from 150 to 550 thousand hives in 2013, and croatia now exports about 2,000 tons of honey. it's a natural way of growing honey without genetically modified substances. it's the kind of honey croatian citizens are used to consuming. that's why i supported the environmental committee's position by voting for an amendment to this report that would require gmo pollen to be listed as an ingredient in honey and not a natural part of it. citizens have a right to know what they're consuming. in fact, the european court of justice itself in the balbok case says that honey containing pollen from genetically modified substances needs special marketing authorization. the health effects of honey are also mentioned. the provision whereby the gmo ingredients of honey should not be specifically highlighted on the packaging would benefit large producers and importers of honey. one that i couldn't support because of the 12,000 beekeepers in croatia, but also across the eu that i mentioned at the beginning. the result of such a directive would be execution for them. if a product retains genetically modified ingredients, consumers need to know this, so such a product should be labelled as containing gmos. the consumer is then given the right to choose between two types of product.
in writing. − i fully support the position voted by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, which endorses the position of the european court of justice by legally classifying pollen from gmos as an ingredient of honey, rather than a natural constituent of it. this approach will protect the consumerʼs freedom of choice regarding pollen produced from gmos, protect the beekeeping sector in its efforts to produce gmo-free honey, exempt honey from bearing a list of ingredients, etc. honey is not produced and sold for the beekeepers nor its importers, but for consumers who wish to consume high quality gmo-free honey. in that regard, consumers need to be clearly informed about what they are potentially buying and consuming. this position will ensure the existence of beekeepers in all member states and nearly 9 000 small beekeepers in croatia. it will ensure that citizens of the european union, and thus croatian citizens, are able to consume high-quality honey along with the opportunity to choose between gmo and gmo-free food through labelling.
written. - i commend the efforts of rapporteur girling to bring common sense back into the business of beekeepers, mainly small and medium-sized enterprises, across europe. in particular, after the european court of justice ruled in 2011 that pollen is an ingredient of honey, the same decision caused costly and unnecessary complications for beekeepers who found themselves in the situation of having to relabel all honey and honey-containing products to indicate pollen as an ingredient in the same. the same practice has the potential to cost beekeepers eur 3,25 million, while undermining the consumer's perception of honey as a natural product. as honey is a natural product, it should be exempted from the obligation to display the list of ingredients. that is why i voted for the amendment by rapporteur girling, which calls for pollen to be considered not as an ingredient of honey but as a constituent of the plant.

on behalf of the ecr club. madam president, homelessness is an attack on human dignity and as a mass phenomenon it has no place in 21st century europe. but trends show that we are not moving in the desired direction and that the rise of homelessness is a european reality at this moment. i therefore support the adoption of a strategy to tackle homelessness, but i believe it is very important that it is thorough and comprehensive. the increase in homelessness in the european union is the result of a number of social problems, primarily the result of the economic crisis, to which we have not found an adequate response. i will only give a croatian example: every day, a dozen families lose their property, mostly the properties in which they live, because they are subject to an enforcement procedure. croatia has adopted a very strong and effective legislative framework for debt collection from over-indebted citizens in recent years, but has failed to incorporate a social component. the consequence of putting the state exclusively on the side of the creditors in such cases, without looking at the broader social picture, is the growing number of croatian families who have been left without a roof over their heads and thus become a burden on the social system. the state, as the debt collector, ultimately burdens itself while ensuring the unconditional collection of private creditors, which is a paradox. in these cases, the personal responsibility of those who have found themselves in financial trouble should not be overlooked, but i believe that banks must finally accept business risk as something most normal in the free market. social systems in some other member states are under great pressure from the growing number of immigrants, which is a very different kind of problem from the one in croatia. that is why i believe that this strategy must be comprehensive and offer a wide range of solutions to the growing problem of homelessness in the european union.

written. − freedom of movement for workers is one of the four fundamental freedoms of the eu and is enshrined in article 45 tfeu. it shall entail the abolition of discrimination based on nationality between workers of the member states in respect of employment, remuneration and other conditions of work and employment. in the context of current debates in some eu member states on the possibilities of restricting the right of free movement for citizens coming from recent member states, e.g. bulgaria, romania and poland, it is important to emphasise that they have gone through a transitional period under the formula (2+3+2 years) during which conditions restricting the freedom of movement of workers were applied. the republic of croatia also agreed in the accession negotiations to a similar formula, which aims to gradually introduce the free movement of workers in the member states over a period of seven years. i believe that the rhetoric and eventual announcements of measures aimed at restricting freedom of movement do not contribute to good relations between countries and are contrary to the eu acquis. taking into account the fact that only around 2,8% of the total eu population benefits from this freedom, it is necessary to recall that freedom of movement within the eu member states is one of the key achievements of the union. the commission should also be able to monitor the implementation of the union's financial instruments and to monitor the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance.

mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, bringing the european union closer to its citizens is also a central problem of european integration. this is best seen in the run-up to the european parliament elections. citizens want to feel, in their daily lives, firsthand what it means to be a citizen of the european union and what positive changes and added value it brings. if we are talking about the right to freedom of movement in any member state as one of those potential positive changes that citizens hope for, then we must definitely consider this motion for a resolution as a step forward in achieving those objectives. enabling people and businesses to move, live, study and work freely without excessive formal and bureaucratic burdens is a necessary prerequisite for the establishment of the single market. in order to achieve this, it is necessary to establish a certain degree of trust and coordination between member states. one of the aims of this proposal is precisely that. it reflects the need of people and business within the european union, as commissioner reding pointed out in her introduction. the mechanisms for achieving this kind of trust are very well developed in this proposal, but it should be stressed that, on the other hand, more efforts are needed to develop mechanisms to prevent possible abuses of the simplification of the adoption of public documents, which could potentially undermine this trust between member states.
mr president, vice-president karas, ms commissioner reding, today's report, presented to us by mr rapkay, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the promotion of freedom of movement for citizens and businesses by facilitating the adoption of certain public documents within the european union, goes to the very heart of what we call one of the four fundamental freedoms, which is the freedom of movement of persons. the fact is that today, after more than 60 years of joint cooperation, we must make efforts to facilitate the freedom of movement and the recognition of documents for our citizens in the simplest and least costly way possible, through legislative proposals like this one, at a horizontal level. as a former diplomat and attorney, i am well versed in the business of legalization and apostille. we all know that they require both time and cost, and the fact is that it is estimated that this act alone should save more than eur 330 million. this is not a small amount of money, but a considerable relief for our citizens in situations where documents are recognised, whether it be copies, birth certificates, marriage certificates or a range of other legal documents that they can and must use in other member states. this would also avoid indirect discrimination. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the measure is compatible with the internal market. i therefore believe that, while maintaining legal certainty and ensuring good control and verification, it is precisely this kind of act at european union level that will make life easier for our citizens. answer the question posed by raising the blue card. thank you, dear colleague rübig, you have now highlighted one of these operational issues, which i mentioned in my speech, namely how to alleviate both costs and administrative obstacles for citizens, especially when it comes to treating patients in other member states. i believe that this proposal is in search of such opportunities and facilitation and, of course, i believe that this requires an additional anagram from the european commission and our rapporteur, because these are the examples where citizens would feel that legislative action, here specifically secondary action, makes their lives easier. i support your suggestion.
mr. president, we face bureaucratic obstacles in our lives every day. the degree of accessibility and serviceability of the bureaucracy varies from one member state to another. in some of them, the battle of the counters and the receipts is a real nightmare. it is even more difficult for foreigners, citizens of other countries, who do not speak the language and do not know the administrative practices of the host country. the european union is often seen as a bureaucratic apparatus that is not happy until it regulates everything from vacuum cleaners to light bulbs, from birth to death. this report is an opportunity to show our citizens how the union can ease their administrative burden and life outside their home member state. i therefore support the measures in this report, such as the abolition of the mandatory certification of photocopies and the unnecessary payment of certified translations. simplified procedures for the cross-border acceptance of public documents will save citizens a lot of time, nerves and money.
mr president, more than 12.5 million citizens in the european union live outside their country of origin, in other member states, and this is, of course, the fruit of freedom of movement. however, that freedom can also be limited by oversized, overpriced, overcomplicated administration. often member states require citizens to provide certified translations of official documents, and this of course makes it more expensive not only for citizens but also for the business community and their businesses. according to the european commission, almost 100 000 documents need to be certified annually because of such requirements by the member states. i therefore support this report and the commission's proposal to end the practice of requiring certified translations. i think it's good for our citizens and, of course, for our businesses and the competitiveness of our economy.
mr president, commissioner, one of the objectives at eu level is to increase and integrate eu mobility. through various policies, such as the youth on the move initiative, it seeks to enhance and standardise the quality of education in particular, so that diplomas and other qualifications can be recognised as easily as possible between member states. however, once such mutual recognition has been achieved, the document verification process is in many cases lengthy and costly. overloaded administration, often degenerating into bureaucracy, makes it very difficult to achieve the fundamental freedoms on which the union is built. i therefore support this report and hope that the need to remove administrative barriers to the authentication, translation and verification of documents will be recognised in all member states.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur again for the work done by himself and by the committee on legal affairs (juri). just as the juri committee’s report says, the commission wants to abolish needless requirements for accepting peoples’ public documents as real in another member state. with such a proposal, citizens will no longer need to get hold of an apostille stamp within the european union. they will no longer have to get legalised versions of their documents. they will no longer need to present a certified copy together with the original public document, and they will no longer need certified translations. we are doing this for many categories of public documents, focusing on the most important ones like birth and parenthood certificates, and this should not be weakened by limiting the types of documents which have a direct impact on cutting red tape for citizens and companies. just speak with people who lead companies in border areas, and they will tell you how much energy and money is lost in useless red tape. that is why the commission cannot accept amendments 50 and 51. of course, we still have safeguards in place against possible fraudulent use of documents, to avoid abuse of the system. this is very important, because the safeguards today are not very high: you can simply forge a document and there is no communication between the administrations in two member states to check whether the document is forged or not, when there is doubt. what we are changing now is that where there is reasonable doubt about the authenticity of a public document, the authorities of the member state where the document is presented may submit, via the internal market information system, a request to the issuing authority for information verifying the authenticity of said document. by the way, administrative cooperation between member states using this tool, which was developed in 2008, has proved its efficiency. it is successfully used under six union legal instruments. it can also be used for the purpose we are discussing today. an additional tool for checking the authenticity of national public documents will be the repository of models of national public documents provided by the imi. this repository will enable member state authorities to carry out the first check on the authenticity of a public document, thereby helping to prevent fraud and forgery. this is very important, because what we are seeing today is an inability to fight fraud. we need to establish this ability, just as we need also to get rid of red tape, which is absolutely unnecessary. i would like to underline – for those who might not have read the report by the juri committee – that our measures do not deal with the recognition of the effects or, in other words, with the content of those public documents.

written. - trade in substances and mixtures is not only a matter of the internal market, but also of the global market. in order to facilitate trade worldwide, while protecting human health and the environment, harmonised classification and labelling criteria, together with the general principles for their application, have been carefully developed over a period of 12 years within the united nations framework. the result is called the globally harmonized system of classification and labelling of chemicals. the clp regulation establishes general packaging standards to ensure the safe delivery of dangerous substances or mixtures. the correct labelling of hazardous substances and mixtures shall enable the hazard classification to be communicated to the user of the substance or mixture in order to alert the user to the hazard present and the need to avoid exposure and the resulting risks. for this reason, i support the amendment of council directives 92/58/eec, 92/85/eec, 94/33/ec, 98/24/ec and directive 2004/37/ec of the european parliament and of the council to align them with regulation (ec) no 1272/2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures, but i also share the rapporteur's view that all five directives need to be recast in order to provide coherent legislation and health and safety levels when it comes to hazardous chemicals and other substances.

written. - the principle of subsidiarity is a general principle of the european union which regulates the union's competences. the concept of subsidiarity was introduced by the european parliament exactly 30 years ago, in february 1984, when it adopted the draft treaty on european union. today, 30 years later, this report proposes further steps in the development of legislation, in the context of the expansion of the democratic legitimacy of the european union and the preservation of the european union's social acquis. further steps to regulate this issue should be taken to facilitate the whole procedure on which subsidiarity is based it often happens that due to short deadlines or lack of funds national parliaments cannot properly implement this principle and in the future this procedure should be improved and made more efficient. i also agree that more attention should be paid to the system of timely involvement of national parliaments in a balanced way that does not represent an inefficient proportion of additional bureaucracy. any attempt to regulate the principle of subsidiarity more effectively for the mutual benefit of the european institutions and national parliaments is worth supporting.

written. - unlike weapons of mass destruction and landmines, the trade in conventional weapons was not regulated by legally binding international regulations. the arms trade treaty (att) intends to change that flaw. the arms trade treaty establishes a common international standard for regulating international trade in conventional arms, and to some extent, ammunition and component parts. the att has established the first global regulation of the legal trade in firearms, which will prevent illegal trade. it will also help to counter international terrorism and organised crime, and curb serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. furthermore, the treaty regulates the trade in the types of weapons most commonly used in local wars, terrorist attacks and coups. member states are required to establish a national control system for arms transfers and for assessing the risk that these arms could endanger peace and security or be used to commit violations of international humanitarian law, human rights and terrorism. for this reason, i support this report and express the hope that it will contribute to disarmament and arms control.

written. - action at european union level is necessary to maintain the proper functioning of the internal market. entrepreneurs increasingly have cross-border activities that need to be regulated by eu legislation. council regulation no 1346/2000 on insolvency proceedings is based on the fact that, due to the wide disparities in substantive law, it is not possible to introduce insolvency proceedings with a uniform scope throughout the union. this also applies to the very different laws on pledge rights in the community. i consider that specific rules on the applicable law should be provided for in the case of particularly significant rights and legal relationships (e.g. rights in rem and employment contracts). the national proceedings (including only assets in the state of the proceedings) should also be allowed alongside the main insolvency proceedings with a single scope. in order to make insolvency proceedings with cross-border effects more effective, it is necessary to consolidate the provisions on jurisdiction, recognition and the law applicable in this field in a single community legal act. it should be binding and directly applicable in the member states. in conclusion, i would like to stress the good functioning of this regulation, even 10 years after its entry into force.
written. - the reporter did a quality job when it came to this report. such regulations are of great interest to business entities as they contribute to a clearer interpretation of bankruptcy proceedings when it comes to companies with ownership or debts located in more than one country. in bankruptcy proceedings, and in particular in pre-bankruptcy settlements, creditors are normally the ones who should be in a more favourable position. however, if in a composition procedure the debtor decides on the process independently, the creditors are placed at a very disadvantage. such a process is socially very dangerous because there are cases, as for example in croatia, where debtors themselves become the largest "creditor" and a situation is created in which settlement proceedings are decided not by creditors but by debtors. in the case of croatia, where pre-bankruptcy settlements are worth almost eur 6,38 billion, the epilogue takes on a broader scope when we understand that the settlement procedure is led by a settlement board appointed by the minister of finance, and it is the ministry of finance that is often one of the main creditors. i would like to say that the unification of bankruptcy proceedings is a good thing not only for businesses but also for member states and their citizens. in this way, we want to make it known that laws that are not in the interest of society, and this is clearly seen in the example of croatia, must be changed and brought into line with general norms at the union level.
written. - cross-border insolvency proceedings occur when the debtor's assets or liabilities are located in more than one country or if the debtor is subject to the jurisdiction of the courts in more than one country. i voted in favour of this report because its purpose is to improve the efficiency of the opening of insolvency proceedings for the resolution of cross-border cases and to ensure the smoother functioning of the internal market and stability in the context of the economic crisis.

- written. i support these legal acts. the overall objective of the commission was that by the end of the 7th parliamentary term, all provisions referring to the regulatory procedure with scrutiny should be removed from all legislative instruments. the commission put forward three proposals for a regulation adapting to article 290 tfeu a number of legal acts providing for the use of the regulatory procedure with scrutiny. in this proposal, the commission has analysed more than 30 legislative acts containing rps measures and has come to the conclusion that some of those measures do not fall within the scope of article 290 tfeu. in cases where the commission has considered that those measures fulfil the criteria of article 291 tfeu, it has proposed that the commission be empowered to adopt implementing acts (annex ii). in other cases, the commission proposes to delete those provisions (annex iii). the rapporteur and the specialised committees do not agree with those conclusions. the committee on legal affairs adopted, initiative report which proposes inter alia a set of criteria for application of articles 290 and 291 tfeu.

written. - i support this report but also point out several indisputable facts relating to the problem of the implementation of the article in question of the treaty of lisbon. for the sake of legal perfection and the use of legally relevant terminology, it should be borne in mind that the name of the new comitology is actually a remnant of the old name from the pre-lisbon period, to put it mildly. the changes brought about by the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon have been in the direction of conferring powers on the union bodies in terms of delegated and implementing acts respectively. i consider this topic to be worthy of attention because it is precisely this distinction between delegated and implementing acts that has remained undefined in the treaty. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the new rules on the basis of the information provided by the member states. it should be noted that it is precisely the vague nature of the 'new comitology' that leads to a loss of time in negotiations, so that the legislative procedure is sometimes prolonged precisely because of this issue, and not necessarily because of the content of the negotiations.
written. - 15 years ago, in 1999, with the decision on comitology, the european union took another big step in the field of strengthening the transparency and democratic nature of its functioning. the european parliament was given the right to control the implementation of certain adopted legislative acts, and in 2006 this decision was extended and a new system was introduced a regulatory procedure with scrutiny. in adopting the new set of regulations on comitology, the commission undertook to assess how many of the legislative provisions relating to this procedure remain in force, and the very acts the commission proposes are generalised in application and aim to supplement certain non-essential parts of the legislation. in line with the already agreed direction of legislative initiatives related to the new legal framework, i support these five legislative acts aimed at regulatory harmonisation.

written. - the treaty of lisbon distinguishes between the power of the european commission to adopt non-legislative acts of general application supplementing certain non-essential segments of a legislative act, as provided for in article 290 tfeu in the delegation procedure. the european parliament protects the interests of citizens throughout the european union and has the duty to represent each of them. i take this opportunity to express my concern that many of the people with whom we deal on a daily basis believe that the treaty of lisbon, which was supposed to simplify the complex procedures of the union, has done the opposite and complicated them. however, what i am pointing out is that it is precisely the vagueness of the article in question, as well as article 291, that is causing confusion among citizens. so we all have to make a big effort together to make the processes understandable to the citizens. i welcome and approve of any initiative to define and simplify or clarify the existing situation in order to make the rules consistent. i therefore support this report.

madam president, we cannot but express concern that the delegation of legislative powers to the commission involves important political and strategic issues. in accordance with the treaty of lisbon and with settled case-law, the adoption of the provisions crucial to the question of delegation is a matter for the exclusive competence of the legislator, which means that the adoption of provisions requiring political decisions falling within the legislator's responsibilities cannot be delegated, but can only consist in supplementing or amending non-essential parts of a legislative act. it is recalled that in the field of employment and social affairs, parliament challenged the validity of the eures decision before the european court of justice in order to protect its powers because the commission had not respected the limitations arising from article 291 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. i support the practical proposals aimed at protecting parliament's prerogatives by emphasising the discretion of this body to decide which secondary elements of a legislative act it wants to deal with and which it will not deal with by delegation of power.
madam president, parliament and the council can delegate part of their powers to the european commission under the treaty of lisbon. the adoption of provisions requiring political decisions falling within the responsibility of the legislator may not be delegated, but non-essential parts of a legislative act may be supplemented or amended. the basic act shall specify the purpose, content, scope and duration of the delegation and shall lay down the conditions governing the delegation of power. i voted in favour of this report because it makes a number of concrete and practical recommendations which will contribute to more effective supervision by the member states of the commission's exercise of its implementing powers. the report also highlights the need to strengthen the role of the european parliament in order to give democratic legitimacy to the european commission's delegated acts, which i fully agree with.

states to ensure that young people receive a good quality job offer, continuing education, as well as an apprenticeship or traineeship, within four months of leaving school or remaining unemployed. this is a very practical objective which the european union and the member states have set themselves to tackle youth unemployment. it is a good example of how the european union can help. we have concentrated our efforts on a specific measure aimed at action at national level. the implementation of the youth guarantees should be supported by a substantial contribution from the european union's resources. it is also a concrete example of how the union can help support actions at national level. the member states, assisted by the commission, are now drawing up their implementation plans. more than half the member states have already submitted their plans. the commission will assess them and offer its contribution. it is, of course, up to the member states to adopt the right policies to offer young people a brighter future. the european union can help and provide financial support, but its action and initiatives alone cannot solve the overall problem. we all know that the present economic situation, although gradually improving, remains difficult. the economic environment is not yet conducive to job creation. much of the problem of youth unemployment today is not structural but cyclical. the aim must therefore be to ensure that the level of structural unemployment among young people will soon be at least equal to, if not lower than, that which existed before the crisis. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. the first is the european alliance for apprenticeships. this initiative aims to bring together different areas of existing actions under a common framework, promote the benefits of successful apprenticeship projects and encourage ways in which they could be developed. the other initiative currently under discussion is the proposal for a framework for quality practice. we expect it to be adopted in march at the next employment council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am sure that all these measures are helping to reverse the negative trend in youth unemployment rates. however, much more needs to be done, while at the same time the contributions of other policy areas are needed. these include adapting education systems to market needs and facilitating access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises. it is also important that our economies as a whole return to sustainable growth, which can help create jobs. to achieve this goal, we need to work together and cooperate closely.
member of the commission. - mr president, millions of young people are struggling today to gain a foothold in the european labour market. at present, 5.5 million people in europe under the age of 25 are unemployed and a total of 7.5 million are not in employment, education or training (neets). if we count those aged between 25 and 29 as well, the number of neets rises to over 14 million. urgent action is therefore needed, both to improve the lives of europe’s young generation here and now, and to put a stop to the long-term scarring effects of unemployment at this early stage in people’s working lives. this is why, on the initiative of the commission, the council adopted in april 2013 a recommendation on establishing a youth guarantee, which calls on member states to ensure that all young people under the age of 25 receive either a good-quality offer of employment, an apprenticeship or a traineeship, or the chance to continue their education, within four months of becoming unemployed or leaving formal education. the youth guarantee represents a new, integrated, approach to youth employment, to bring public authorities (employment and education ministries), social partners, ngos, employment services and young people themselves together to tackle the issue in the most efficient and effective way possible. a key facet of the youth guarantee is that it aims to cover all young people, including those who are hardest to help. in order to make this a reality, a serious commitment to outreach work is necessary. so where do we stand today? last june, the european council asked the 20 member states eligible for extra funding under the youth employment initiative to submit youth guarantee implementation plans by december 2013. so far we have received 19 plans. the united kingdom is missing and has promised to submit theirs by the end of february. the eight other member states should submit their implementation plans by the spring of this year. over the last few weeks, the commission has held a series of bilateral meetings with the member states to discuss their plans. our assessment is based on the central elements of the council’s youth guarantee recommendation and, of course, the feasibility for member states to deliver. we are therefore looking for partnership-based approaches; early intervention and activation mechanisms; measures for labour market integration; appropriate and effective use of eu funds; and evaluation mechanisms. as you all know, member states that are eligible for money from the youth employment initiative are required to put in place a strategic policy framework for promoting youth employment, including through implementation of the youth guarantee. this is the so called ex-ante conditionality, whose purpose is to help to ensure the high quality and effectiveness of investments financed from the youth employment initiative and the european social fund. each member state’s youth guarantee implementation plan is therefore expected to be the key part of this strategic policy framework. investing our efforts in the quality of the youth guarantee implementation plans now is important in order for member states to be ready and able to roll out the youth guarantee and effectively utilise the available eu funding. it is also important to get the implementation plans right, otherwise we cannot achieve the intended results. to contribute to the implementation of the youth guarantee – and the provision of quality offers of work opportunities for young people – the commission presented a council recommendation on a quality framework for traineeships. the quality framework proposes guidelines for traineeships outside educational curricula, and aims to ensure fair working conditions and high quality learning content so that traineeships serve as real stepping stones from education to employment. member states are now negotiating the proposal for a council recommendation with a view to achieving adoption by the march council of employment and social affairs ministers. unfortunately, a group of member states seem to disagree with these objectives as they are seeking to water down the proposal. these member states put in question whether the quality framework should deal with working conditions. some do not want to limit the duration of traineeships and some also wish to weaken all references to the implementation of the quality framework. of course this approach is a significant disappointment for me and raises important questions for the future. how to explain such a move in the council when the european council itself had called on the commission to propose a quality framework on traineeships? i therefore call for your support to raise your voice against such a dilution of the initiative. another complementary initiative to support the youth guarantee is the european alliance for apprenticeships launched in july last year. this seeks to improve the quality and supply of apprenticeships across the eu and to change attitudes to apprenticeships by promoting the benefits of apprenticeship systems. i encourage the member states, social partners and businesses to scale up their activities on apprenticeships, including creating more and better places in member states where companies’ commitment to training young people is not yet well developed. so what happens next? the commission’s analysis of member states’ endeavours on the youth guarantee is feeding into the european semester process. the commission is continuing its contacts with member states to ensure they deliver the main axis of the guarantee and therefore may adjust their implementation plans at the latest when submitting their national reform programmes in mid-april. the council of employment and social affairs ministers on 10[nbsp ]march will be an opportunity to discuss implementation of the youth guarantee with ministers, and on 8[nbsp ]april the commission is organising a high-level conference in brussels to take stock of the implementation of the youth guarantee. this will also be an opportunity to highlight the reforms being undertaken as well as the common challenges. the full roll-out of comprehensive youth guarantee schemes will require substantial funding. it is now crucial to proceed with speedy programming of the european social fund and youth employment initiative activities. member states need to take full advantage of the frontloading of the youth employment initiative budget commitments to 2014 and 2015. the common provisions regulation provides the possibility for early adoption of dedicated youth employment initiative operational programmes that can be up and running even before the adoption of the partnership agreement. this opportunity to prepare a dedicated specific operational programme should be seriously considered by member states as it allows time to be saved when addressing youth unemployment challenges through the youth employment initiative. we should also bear in mind that pre-financing may only be released and funding reimbursed to member states once the operational programmes are adopted. this is why swift programming is crucial. but, until the operational programmes are adopted, member states should also consider the fact that the eligibility date for youth employment initiative expenditure is 1[nbsp ]september 2013. therefore, member states could use this opportunity by mobilising national funding for youth employment initiative related activities already now, as the expenditure would be reimbursed subsequently under the adopted operational programmes. yet, while european funds can help, we also need to see national funds being committed to maximise impact and coverage, and really make a difference for young people. to conclude, the implementation of the youth guarantee is proceeding through intensive efforts and we must not relax our high ambitions. i encourage member states to maintain their high level of engagement to make a real difference to the lives of the many young people who are currently struggling.

mr president, i supported the proposal to introduce an interoperable e-call system which requires that all cars manufactured after october 2015 must have devices connected to the single european union emergency number, 112, which will automatically alert this number for emergencies in the event of an accident. according to the commission, e-call can speed up the response of emergency services by 40% in urban areas and by 50% in rural areas. these are significant increases that can certainly be of great help in saving lives. today, less than 1% of vehicles are equipped with e-calling, and that's mostly luxury cars. rapid access to emergency care must be the right of all, not just the rich. every year 28 000 people die on european roads, and the price of this device for the manufacturer is 50 euros, and i think that's a small price to pay for potentially saving lives.
mr. chairman, today less than 1% of transportation is equipped with e-prospect. in addition to the need to develop emergency centres and make e-calling mandatory in new means of transport, the european commission has decided to oblige member states to adapt their operations and enable e-calling in all vehicles by 2015. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the conditions for the use of the information referred to in paragraph 1 of this article. the republic of croatia has experience with the introduction of the ecall service and call centre and this is in place in our country, along with the czech republic and romania, and this system was introduced voluntarily. our experience shows that the introduction of an interoperable e-call system is extremely important for saving lives and i was pleased to support this report today.

written. - this regulation, which allows member states to compensate railway undertakings for the payment of certain obligations, was adopted before the liberalisation of the railway market and while railways were mostly developing within national borders, with integrated undertakings and infrastructure management. i would remind you that the european rail sector has been losing market share for the last 60 years and that research has shown that many railway companies rely on public subsidies. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market within the meaning of article 107 (3) (c) of the treaty. however, what is obvious is the restrictive nature of the regulation that only certain undertakings are listed in the regulation, to be precise a few dozen of them, out of over a thousand railway undertakings in europe. in view of the current climate of lack of funding, it would not be a bad idea to retain the possibility of compensation to railway undertakings, but in this case, to leave this possibility to all railway undertakings. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties.
in writing. - i vote in favour regarding the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council repealing regulation (eec) no 1192/69 of the council on common rules for the normalisation of the accounts of railway undertakings. in the framework of the fourth railway package, the commission proposes to remove rules regarding normalisation of the accounts of railway undertakings. it allows member states to compensate railway undertakings for payment of obligations which transport modes do not have to support. within these obligations can be special payments in cases of accidents at work and pensions of workers who retire earlier. since 2007 four member states have made use of this regulation; belgium, germany, ireland and poland. the commission thinks that the regulation no longer respects the legal environment.
in writing. - regulation (eec) no[nbsp ]1192/69 was adopted before the rail market was liberalised and when rail transport in europe was developing primarily within national borders, with integrated companies both operating rail services and managing rail infrastructure. at the time, the objective of the regulation was to put railway undertakings in other transport modes on an equal competitive footing. i voted in favour of this proposal, which aims to repeal regulation (eec) no[nbsp ]1192/69. in all previous railway packages, as proposed by the commission and then adopted and transposed by member states, the aim was to extend rights and obligations to all the rail newcomers and thus to open up the rail market. here, the commission proposes to solve potential discrimination among railway undertakings not by an appropriate recast, as in the case of other legislative texts, but by directly deleting the act: i.e. by repealing the regulation.

vice-president of the commission. - mr[nbsp ]president, members, firstly, on the melo report: the commission takes very good note of the agreement reached between parliament and the council on this initiative of member states, introducing a european investigation order in criminal matters. this directive, if it is properly implemented and used, can be a good tool to fight cross-border crime and help to bring suspected criminals to justice. this directive seeks to replace the eu convention on mutual legal assistance and the european evidence warrant framework decision. i just wish to underline that the latter was adopted by the council in 2008, and implemented in two member states only. the commission hopes this time things will be different. it expects member states to implement the directive correctly and on time, so that it will not become a dead letter, as was the case with the european evidence warrant. recently the commission published a report on the implementation of three pre-lisbon framework decisions in the field of detention. these three eu laws focus on mutual recognition of sentences, pre-trial supervision orders and probation orders. the rules aim to improve mutual trust between judicial systems in europe, and this mutual trust is essential in order for a common european area of justice to function. despite the implementation dates being long past, about half of the member states have not transposed these framework decisions into their domestic law. the objective of developing an area of freedom, security and justice for all citizens, as laid down in article[nbsp ]3 of the treaty, can only be achieved if member states do properly implement the instruments they have agreed upon. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr[nbsp ]nuno melo, and his shadow rapporteurs for their very good work. the commission applauds their work in rebalancing this instrument, and in particular their strong advocacy for strengthening the fundamental rights safeguards it contains. this was very helpful and it once again highlights the importance of the european parliament in the co-decision procedure. on the report by sarah ludford: at a recent debate in this chamber, and on numerous other occasions, i have strongly defended the right of european citizens to freedom of movement within the eu. but open borders do not mean that criminals can evade justice simply by travelling to another member state. that is why we have the european arrest warrant – in effect since 2004. it is an efficient tool for surrendering people suspected of an offence from one eu country to another. it makes sure that neither suspects nor convicted criminals can hide in the european area of justice. we have many examples: dozens of suspected drug smugglers, murderers and child-sex offenders, for instance, have been brought back to the uk from spain in very short time[nbsp ]spans, and this would not have been possible before the european arrest warrant. likewise, thanks to the european arrest warrant, many suspected terrorists are now answering for their alleged crimes in the jurisdictions where they were wanted. the european arrest warrant is a very successful criminal justice instrument. that does not mean, however, that it is perfect or that these operations cannot be improved. the commission has said – and i recall the 2011 implementation report – that there is room for improvement, for instance, in order to avoid the use of the european arrest warrant for crimes that are not very serious, and paying due regard to fundamental rights. in this context, i would like to thank the rapporteur, ms[nbsp ]ludford, and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) for the work they have done and the expertise that has gone into this report. we will closely consider the issues raised in the report, which will feed into the permanent ongoing work on improving the european arrest warrant system. we are already in the process of addressing some of the issues raised by the report. for instance, on the issues around fundamental rights, the commission has worked to strengthen the rights of defendants. the now agreed directives on the right to interpretation and translation, on the right to information about rights, and on the right of access to a lawyer, constitute minimum standards throughout the eu. i only regret that some member states do not want to participate in this system of minimum rights throughout the eu, because these rights represent a counterbalance to the important tool of the european arrest warrant. for instance, persons subject to an arrest warrant will have a lawyer in both the issuing and the executing member state. if you do not apply the rules, then of course the people who are taken on a european arrest warrant will not have that right. that is why i regret very much that some member states do not want to participate in implementing these fundamental rights. the european parliament has been a driving force and a key partner in delivering the three directives on procedural rights. i want to thank parliament for that. i also welcome the start of the european parliament’s work on the commission’s recent proposals on legal aid, presumption of innocence, procedural rights for children and vulnerable suspects, which will also help to complete the procedural rights roadmap in the future and will be a good complement to the european arrest warrant. i would like to see all these instruments in place and being applied by all member states and i wish to close any remaining gaps in the protection of fair-trial rights across europe. in your report, the european arrest warrant is correctly placed in the wider context of the mutual recognition instruments – the framework decisions dealing with the mutual recognition of sentences, probation orders and pre-trial supervision orders. as i said at the beginning, the commission has adopted an implementation report in which we observed that these decisions have not been fully transposed by member states. against that background the commission considers that a decision to re-open the european arrest warrant would be premature. because, despite repeated calls by the commission to member states, the european arrest warrant has not yet received the benefit of full implementation of the complementary mutual-recognition instruments. once the commission has full infringement powers to act on the transposition and implementation of these instruments – and that will be the case from december this year – we will work towards full implementation. this will be the case in respect of instruments such as the european supervision order, which can help to reduce pre-trial detention in european arrest warrant cases. in your report, you also request eu funding for training and networks for the european arrest warrant. that request is most welcome and is already being met in a number of projects. we will continue these efforts. we also share the report’s focus on the importance of reliable data. to that end the commission has developed and agreed with member states a new questionnaire seeking european arrest warrant data. let me assure you that your valuable work will feed into our efforts on the common goal of improving the european arrest warrant system.

written. - i supported the report by mr lehne and mr berlinguer on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the common european law on the sale of goods (cesl). during the lithuanian presidency, this project was one of the council's priorities, which was pushed for rapid adoption despite the cautious approach of the european parliament. the aim is to align cesl with national legislation and the treaty of lisbon. the non-binding nature of this instrument is confirmed and it is concluded that cesl and national legislation can coexist. the scope of the tool has been reduced in relation to distance selling, but has been extended in relation to digital content through the inclusion of online contracts, and in line with the priorities of the europe 2020 strategy which aims to ensure inclusive and sustainable growth by enhancing the digital agenda of the european union. the level of consumer protection is in line with the lisbon treaty and is satisfactory from a legal point of view as it improves legal remedies for consumers. this trade-off will facilitate the business of smes and reduce costs and strengthen trade in the internal market. contract law is one of the epp group's priorities, and so is cesl, which i supported at first reading.
in writing. - i agree with the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on a common european sales law. contract law barriers prevent consumers and traders from fully harnessing internal market potential, in particular in distance selling. it is necessary to have a single uniform set of contract law rules in all member states in order to overcome these barriers. a common european sales law should represent an addition, increasing the choice available to parties and the possibility of its use whenever will help facilitate cross-border trade and reduce opportunity costs. it should become the basis when parties decide to use it. it would be advisable for the common european sales law to be available for cross-border contracts, to minimise complexity and additional costs. cross-border contracts should be determined on the basis of the habitual residence of both parties, in business to business relations.
written. - differences in the laws of individual countries make cross-border trade more complex and expensive than internal. the costs for smes to enter foreign markets can become twice as high as their overall earnings and they therefore very quickly give up their intention to engage in cross-border trade. the common european law on the sale of goods, which simplifies cross-border transactions in the single market, gives sellers the choice to sell their products in another member state under a single set of contract law rules that could be considered as an alternative to the national contract law in force in each member state. although the commission proposal covers a set of contractual rights, it does not regulate a number of important factors, and thus creates risks for business in foreign countries in the form of legal advice fees and the lack of provisions relating to the transfer of ownership. accordingly, i do not support the proposal for a common european law on the sale of goods because i believe that the creation of a new legal instrument with the possibility of leaving the choice in the hands of the seller could complicate the legal situation and discriminate against the buyer. i propose that the existing process of adapting consumer rights should be continued and improved.

in writing. - indonesia is the first and the largest timber exporting country in asia to sign the flegt-vpa with the eu. the flegt-vpa aims to halt the trade of illegal timber and ensure that only verified legal timber and timber products are imported to the eu from indonesia. the agreement concerns a licensing system for timber products exported from indonesia to any of the 28 eu member states, based on the wood legality verification system (svlk), the first national timber legality assurance system in the world to be implemented based on flegt principles. once the flegt-vpa is fully operational and flegt licenses are issued, indonesian timber products will be acknowledged to be in full compliance with the eu timber regulation number 995/2010, which prohibits the placement of illegal timber on the eu market. operators and traders will not have to conduct a due diligence process on timber legality for flegt licensed products. i welcome this agreement which is a significant breakthrough that represents the strategic cooperation between producing and consuming countries.

written. - i support this motion. in the last decade, the extraterritorial use of drones with deadly consequences has been steadily increasing. thousands of civilians have been killed or seriously injured as a result of drone strikes. i believe that there is not enough transparency and that there are often no adequate investigations into incidents arising from the use of such aircraft. we need to ban extrajudicial targeted killings using these weapons and i think the european commission should show data on all research and projects related to drones that are funded by eu funds. we need to create a legal framework for the use of armed drones to prevent misuse and increase transparency.
in writing. - the use of drones in armed conflicts has increased significantly in recent years, raising humanitarian, legal and other concerns. most military drones are used for intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance, as well as target acquisition. under international humanitarian law – the rules of war, i.e. the set of laws governing armed conflicts – drones are not expressly prohibited, nor are they considered to be inherently indiscriminate or perfidious. in this respect, they are no different from weapons launched from manned aircraft such as helicopters or other combat aircraft. it is important to emphasise, however, that while drones are not unlawful in themselves, their use is subject to international law. it is worth pointing out that not all drones are actually armed and used to fight. unarmed surveillance drones can be used for a range of civilian purposes. they can, for example, help detect fires and therefore save lives, or to be used to collect vitally important information for relief personnel working in areas affected by natural disasters. in the future, drones might also help deliver emergency aid in remote areas. in this regard, i voted in favour.

written. - i fully support the report on the recommendations to the commission on the revision of the european arrest warrant. the area of substantive criminal issues, and therefore the procedural part thereof, falls within public law. as such, it is of interest to the wider social community and is the subject of the european acquis. because of the importance of the application of the european arrest warrant in pan-european criminal cooperation, i consider it to be a key institution that should be discussed in order to bring it into line. the european arrest warrant is also special because it is unified in the legislation of the european union, and we know that this is not the case with all the institutions of both procedural and substantive criminal law of the member states of the union. that is why we are talking about harmonisation, not unification of criminal law standards. what i consider to be a high quality aspect of this report is its indicative presentation of the elements of weakness of this institution that may in some situations cause legal uncertainty and its invitation to the commission to submit legislative proposals to address those weaknesses within the time limits provided for in the regulation. i would also like to stress the advantage of the proper application of the european arrest warrant in terms of creating a european judicial culture. however, i note that the revision of this procedural institution must remain an instrument of rationalization, efficiency and cooperation based on respect for the rights of the parties guaranteed by international agreements.
written. - i have supported the report of baroness sarah ludford with recommendations to the commission on the revision of the european arrest warrant. the eun has an important role to play in the framework of judicial cooperation in criminal matters. by replacing the complex extradition procedure, the instrument demonstrates a high degree of mutual trust between member states, simplifies and speeds up the surrender procedure, including that of its own nationals, and contributes to avoiding impunity. over the past 10 years, the european commission has presented three reports on the implementation of the framework decision, and the eun has been globally assessed as a successful instrument. however, the same reports also pointed to certain shortcomings in the functioning of the system as regards procedural rights of suspects, conditions of detention and the application of the principle of proportionality. official statistics confirm that difficulties exist, as 54 689 eun were issued and 11 630 were executed in the period 2005-2009. i believe that the recommendations of this report should be taken into account and that the eu's review should ensure respect for human and fundamental rights. the use of eun should be effective and proportionate and should ensure that the rights of suspects are respected throughout the proceedings. in the context of the example of the republic of croatia, which faced the problem of incorrect transposition of the framework decision upon its accession to the eu, i believe that the european commission should act effectively with regard to the mechanism of control by member states as regards correct transposition into national legislation.
in writing. - the european arrest warrant is the most important eu legal instrument based on common recognition, where judicial decisions are made on the basis of mutual trust. the aim of this framework is to make the process of bringing suspects and accused persons to justice faster and easier. the member state has to execute the warrant without any assessment of the substance of the accusation. since it was introduced, it has provided a more efficient mechanism to ensure that those who seek to evade justice are not able to exploit open borders. still, the framework also has negative sides, such as poor detention conditions, alleged overuse of european arrest warrants by some member state and failure to apply proportionality. these problems should be solved in order not to undermine the credibility of the european arrest warrant and eu criminal justice initiatives in general. one of the goals of the european union is to promote freedom, security and justice. it is crucial to have effective instruments for mutual recognition in order to help us to build an efficient framework for the entire union.
