member of the commission. - mr president, first of all my thanks to ms de keyser – and i must make an admission. this is one of my favourite subjects, because for five years i was a member of the committee for the prevention of torture of the council of europe, which does fieldwork. it does not just discuss in plenary or in meetings, but its members actually visit prisons and prison cells. i was once accidentally locked inside a cell with a prisoner, and the prisoner had to ring for the guards to release me, so they take the job very seriously and do some excellent work. because, as some members of parliament have said, we also have isolated cases of torture, of people in detention in our own countries in the european union. we welcome this report on the eradication of torture, and this is one of the most important rights. if we look at most constitutions, it is put third or fourth in terms of fundamental rights, and it was one of the few rights where there are no exceptions. even the right to life has exceptions, but the right to protection from torture usually does not have any exceptions. while the task of eradicating torture is, unfortunately, far from being achieved, we acknowledge the need to improve the overall coherence of eu policy in combating torture. as this house is well aware, in our fight against torture, we follow a so-called ‘holistic’ approach that encompasses all the essential elements: the prevention of torture, but also the protection and rehabilitation focusing on the victims of torture and ill-treatment. guided by the commitments of the eu action plan on democracy and human rights and also the eu guidelines on torture, we promote the eradication of torture through all bilateral contacts with third countries. in particular, human rights dialogues with 42 states allow us to address individual cases of concern and to encourage the ratification of key international instruments, notably the optional protocol to the un convention against torture: the so-called cat. this being said, our anti-torture policy would be far less effective without the persistent efforts to address torture and ill-treatment within the un framework. in this context, during the ongoing session of the un human rights council, the eu is following the situation in syria, the democratic people’s republic of korea and ukraine with particular attention. in all these cases, it is crucial to ensure accountability for perpetrators of grave human rights violations, including torture, and to provide rehabilitation and relief to victims. we share the view that torture affecting those who are most vulnerable, notably children and women, amounts to one of the most abhorrent violations of human rights. in order to address the root causes of this phenomenon, the eu is engaged in efforts to reduce all forms of violence against children through more effective child protection systems and to raise greater awareness about children’s rights, including their right to freedom from violence. in parallel, in order to prevent the torture of children, the eu asks the partner countries which have lowered the criminal liability age to reconsider their decision. similar efforts are being made to eradicate violence against women, and our recent endeavours focus in particular on the elimination of female genital mutilation. taking good note of the need to improve the targeted use of political tools at our disposal, work is currently ongoing to guide eu diplomats in third countries in their work on eradicating torture. the specific guidance on this important issue will include advice on visits to detention centres, trial monitoring and follow-up to individual cases raised by the european union. at the same time, in line with the request of parliament and civil society, in february this year we revived the council human rights working group task force on torture. the task force will remain an informal network of interested member states providing impetus to the implementation of the eu guidelines on torture. last but not least, our anti-torture policy is effective only if it permeates all the external policies of the union, including development and trade. in this regard, the commission has taken the initiative for a review of council regulation 1236/2005, which restricts trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment or torture. in tabling this proposal, the commission has taken into consideration the european parliament’s views expressed in its resolution of 17[nbsp ]june[nbsp ]2010. regulating eu trade in order to help prevent capital punishment and torture from occurring in third countries is essential and reflects the fundamental values on which the eu is based. however, as we know, such regulation is not sufficient to ensure that third countries abolish capital punishment and to prevent torture from occurring in such countries. other actions, notably dialogue with third countries, and further action at the un general assembly level are also needed to achieve these goals. as you can see, the road to a world free from torture and ill-treatment is a long and difficult one, but i am convinced that, united in our endeavours, we shall continue to make progress.

on behalf of the ppe club. mr president, i welcome commissioner borg and, as shadow rapporteur on behalf of the european people's party, i once again thank my colleague ival kalfin and the other shadow rapporteurs for their efforts in drafting this important decision which, with guarantees from the european union budget, enables the european investment bank to place loans in third countries. the european investment bank is a powerful complementary instrument for the european union's external action and the promotion of both our values and interests in the world. therefore, it seems to me that the objectives we have defined here, namely, first and foremost, supporting regions and other countries in terms of local private sector development to support smes, social and economic infrastructure, climate change mitigation and upgrading all the comparative advantages that the eib has already proven to have, are very constructive in our external action. in this respect, i believe that the regional economic integration of neighbouring countries, particularly those in the pre-accession process, will also be supported by the european investment bank loans. the fact that we were able to negotiate a guarantee of 30 billion euros instead of 28 using the feed-in from svemip showed creativity in the negotiation process. the revision of 30 june 2016 gives us flexibility to see how we prioritise during the second half of this multiannual financial framework and i am particularly pleased that we have put more resources into the country in the pre-accession process, the eastern partnership countries and the mediterranean countries. i would like to look particularly at ukraine in that context, given the circumstances that are currently there today and the positive announcement last week of an eib package of an additional 3 billion over the first 3 years. the commission has also received comments from the ukrainian authorities.
mr. president, the guarantee of losses is by definition the socialization of losses. if you socialize potential loss, it makes sense that you socialize gain. on the other hand, the european investment bank in countries outside the union should serve, and probably does, to stimulate growth in those countries. the european union also benefits in this way. at least partially alleviating the problems of economic immigration, at the same time making these countries better and more reliable partners. we've already talked about surveillance today. but i would stress once again the importance of controlling the absorption of credit and corruption in the countries the bank enters. the comments that investment in other countries is damaging employment in europe are simply not serious and do not stand. we're not going to get richer if those around us are poorer. there are others we should look at with suspicion. the crisis is not the fault of the poor.
mr president, the european investment bank is an important instrument to support and further strengthen the external activities of the european union, and in particular those activities which are in line with our general development principles. in this context, alongside economic and social development, i am thinking in particular of improving environmental protection and eradicating poverty and improving human rights. and it is precisely because of the importance of the european investment bank in achieving the stated objectives of our foreign policy that i must express my regret that the resources allocated in the new multiannual financial framework are not even greater. however, while expressing regret at this fact, i would like to stress two things in particular which are crucial if the funds allocated to the european investment bank are to be spent in the best possible way. in particular, in our external activities, better and more effective cooperation between the european commission, the european external action service and the european investment bank is needed. this is undoubtedly one of the prerequisites for avoiding unnecessary dispersal of resources and for their optimal use. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new financial framework and will continue to monitor the implementation of the new financial framework. in this respect, i fully support the rapporteur's proposal to oblige the european investment bank to publish the registers of all end-users. this will increase the transparency we seek and ensure that the funds of european taxpayers in countries outside our community are used in a responsible and purposeful way.
mr president, i thank the rapporteur and it is a special honour for me and all our representatives from the republic of croatia that our colleague, mr plenkovic, was the shadow rapporteur for this report which was prepared with great care. the eib's activities in countries outside the european union are of particular importance, as reforms and convergence in these countries are encouraged by the provision of favourable financing instruments. this is why it is important to support and encourage the eib to have as much presence and action as possible in countries outside the european union. it is necessary to continue, in the 2014-2020 perspective, the concrete financial support provided through the guarantee to the eib in the event of losses in the financing of investment and development projects outside the union. i support the changes proposed in the report, namely the targeting of guarantees to less creditworthy beneficiaries, stronger financing of climate change projects and a more concrete linking of eib financing with european union policies.
written. - inland ports are key elements of the entire inland waterway transport system. the success of the entire transport process from the place of production to the place of final consumption depends on this system. at the same time, ports are also links between the different modes of transport by which goods or passengers are brought in and taken out to their final destinations. ports are also the driving force behind the development of the country's various economic activities. as a representative from croatia, i believe that inland waterways throughout croatia are given a new framework for development by the adoption of a european action plan at the level of the european union. all problems related to the inland waterway transport sector need to be addressed in a coordinated manner at community level and it is therefore important that croatia actively participates in the statistics on inland waterway freight transport. furthermore, the commission needs statistics on the transport of goods by inland waterways in order to monitor and develop the common transport policy, as well as the transport elements of the policy on regions and on trans-european networks. community statistics on all modes of transport should be compiled in accordance with common standards. this would achieve the greatest possible comparability between modes of transport. in conclusion, i support this report.

the european community and the government of the united states of america are engaged in research and technological activities in a number of areas of mutual interest. the parties shall cooperate in the development of the relevant international standards and standards for the protection of human health and the environment, including the international standard for the protection of human health and the international standard for the protection of new varieties of plants. the formal basis for cooperation in the field of scientific and technological research has been established. they will in future extend and strengthen cooperation activities in areas of common interest and encourage the application of the results of such cooperation to their economic and social benefit. this substantial agreement covers a wide range of areas of cooperation: environment (including climate research), biomedicine and health (including research on aids, communicable diseases and drug abuse), agriculture, fisheries science, technological research, non-nuclear energy, natural resources, materials science and metrology, information and communication technologies, telematics, biotechnology, marine science and technology, social science research, transport, science and technology policy, governance, training and mobility of scientists. finally, i support the extension of the agreement on scientific and technological cooperation between the european community and the government of the united states of america, as cooperation has shown good results in recent years.

the nagoya protocol was adopted at the international congress on biodiversity held in japan on 29 october 2010. the protocol relates to genetic material and resources to which sovereign states claim rights and regulates their use. the three pillars are access to genetic resources, sharing the results of their development and respecting agreed terms. the agreement contains a provision that obliges the signatories to suspend the use of genetic resources if there is a doubt about the legality of the right of access to them. equal access and fair use will encourage biodiversity conservation and development. the nagoya protocol will also greatly benefit european science and industry, which is why i support this report.
in writing. - the nagoya protocol, an international treaty signed by the 28 eu countries, has as its primary objective the equitable sharing of the benefits of energy resources in order to preserve biodiversity and its availability in nature. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the nagoya protocol to include the whole of the mediterranean basin, which is the largest of the mediterranean countries.
written. - i supported the report on access to genetic resources the so-called nagoya protocol and fair sharing of profits. the entry into force of the protocol requires all 28 eu member states to adopt the convention on biological diversity as well as adequate access to reliable genetic resources and fair sharing of benefits. in this way, it contributes to the conservation of biological diversity and the sustainable use of its components in accordance with the objectives of the convention on biological diversity. this establishes a balance between the providers and users of genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with such resources. it is of the utmost importance that only legally acquired genetic resources are secured and used throughout the process. the fact that developed countries dominate both knowledge and the proper use of genetic resources makes the nagoya protocol an important foundation in the fight against illegal sources of genetic resources, especially for users in developed countries. the protocol will be applied to all products and services that are not covered by the protocol. the eu should actively and systematically monitor the implementation of the protocol and ensure a fair sharing of the benefits.
written. - i supported this draft resolution because, after the final deliberations of the convention on biological diversity, it is high time to introduce a framework for access to genetic resources, fair and equitable distribution of wealth while contributing to the conservation of biological diversity. since the protocol itself is a tool against bio-piracy, we certainly need a swift ratification process and its entry into force. but we also need a clear definition of bio-piracy to combat the opaque work of multinational corporations, in terms of plant and gene patenting, the theft of traditional knowledge and practical skills. on the other hand, i supported the draft because the protocol's intention is to explore and conserve the genetic resources in the ecosystem, thereby also contributing to the preservation of the natural signal of biological units. but regardless of the 'in situ' method of conservation, i stress that the use of genetic resources or genetic material from nature must not endanger the survival of the ecosystem or the population of species in their natural habitats.

madam president, i supported the report by my colleagues, mr karinš and ms sargentini, on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing. a revision of the current so-called third anti-money laundering directive of the european union was needed to further strengthen the internal market in order to make financial transfers more transparent in an increasingly complex financial environment and to support the further fight against terrorism and organised crime and the strengthening of the financial system. this type of criminal activity undermines the integrity of the financial sector and the result is, of course, loss of revenue for governments, disruption of market competitiveness and, generally speaking, disruption of the normal functioning of markets and the prevention of development. croatia adopted its law on the prevention of money laundering in 2009 and in this respect cooperates well with both the european union and the council of europe and is working on further efforts to prevent cross-border money laundering activities.
written. - the fight against money laundering in the financial system is of paramount importance to all eu member states, as such activities impede the development of national economies, undermine the integrity and credibility of the financial system and compromise the common market's level playing field, and terrorist financing can have far-reaching consequences beyond the mere economic pursuit of profit. the commission should be able to impose fines on the financial system for infringements of this regulation, including the infringement of the right to privacy and data protection. it is important to assess the money laundering and terrorist financing risks affecting the internal market and this is best done in consultation with member states and supervisory authorities such as the european banking authority, the european insurance and occupational pensions authority and the european securities and markets authority. when talking about better communication between member states and union supervisory authorities, especially in relation to companies involved in cross-border activities, it is important to emphasise the need for better cooperation between member states and supervisory authorities as well as the sharing of information and the interconnection of business registers and their publication to the public and to the responsible authorities. this is one of the prerequisites for minimising illegal activities such as money laundering and terrorist financing.
written. money laundering and terrorist financing are often conducted in an international environment. measures adopted only at national or even european union level, and which do not take into account international coordination and cooperation, have a very limited impact. the measures adopted by the european union in this area should therefore be consistent with other activities undertaken at international level. illicit money flows, and in particular money laundering, represent between 6 and 8.7% of developing countries' gdp, an amount ten times greater than the aid the eu and its member states provide to developing countries. for this reason, the eu must insist on development cooperation to stop the increasing trend of money laundering transfers from developed countries to developing countries with less stringent anti-money laundering legislation. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the definition of the term 'commercial offence' and the definition of the term 'criminal offence'.
written. - the third directive relating to the financial sector requires the identification and verification of parties and beneficial owners and the monitoring of financial transactions. the directive would introduce an obligation to report to competent financial intelligence authorities where there is a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing. according to estimates by the un office on drugs and crime, €330 billion is laundered through illegal activities on an annual basis, with a negative impact on the economies of the eu member states. the primary objective of this directive is to achieve transparency of payment sources and transfers of funds for the purpose of combating terrorism and money laundering while complying with data protection requirements. money laundering seriously affects financial sectors in all world markets and is a major drain on budgets and public finances. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted through state resources and does not distort competition. i support the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council to have an effective impact on the reduction of the abuse of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing.
written. - i supported this report on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing. according to calculations from the international monetary fund, money laundering accounts for up to 5% of global gdp. such criminal activities undermine the integrity of the financial sector, resulting in a loss of revenue for states and distorting competition and negatively affecting the labour market. the registers should be interconnected and accessible to authorities and obliged entities, and member states may grant access to information to other parties and lay down rules on the basis of which the register can be accessed. the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing must be conducted in accordance with the eu legal order, in particular with regard to eu data protection law and the protection of fundamental rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union.
written. - he's working on a deal for a public register of beneficial owners that's been compromised across all political groups. the commission has also received comments from the united kingdom on the application of the principle of proportionality. the achievement of transparency of payment sources and the prevention of the use of the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing is an objective on which all institutions must work together to enable it to be achieved in the interest of all union citizens. however, i find it unacceptable that exceptions are made for certain sectors, or for certain industries such as the gaming industry. the uncontrolled activities of this industry are fertile ground for money laundering, or the conversion of illegal activities into legal ones. although the majority of members voted in favour of allowing member states, with the commission's approval, to exclude certain gambling services from the payment of the commission's fees under the directive because of the allegedly low risk nature of these operations, i will support my group's views that this provision should also be amended in the future.
written. - i support this proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing, which is a revision of the 2005 directive. the changing nature of money laundering and terrorist financing requires the legal framework to combat such threats to be continuously adapted. the objective of this directive is to protect the financial system against money laundering and terrorist financing by means of prevention, investigation and detection measures. these amendments are necessary to strengthen the internal market, to make financial transfers more transparent, to support the fight against terrorism and organised crime and to strengthen the financial system of the european union. according to calculations by the international monetary fund (imf), money laundering is estimated to amount to up to 5[nbsp ]% of global gdp. such criminal activities undermine the integrity of the financial sector, result in lost revenue for governments, disrupt the proper functioning of markets and impede development. however, the approach to prevention through the new directive must be targeted and proportionate and should not imply systematic control of the entire population. of course, the data protection law and the protection of fundamental rights must be respected.
written. - i supported the new proposal for a regulation which calls for improvements to the current framework to prevent the conversion of funds obtained from criminal activities into legitimate funds through the financial system. the flows of dirty money through transfers of funds can damage the stability and reputation of the financial sector and threaten the internal market. terrorism has shaken the very foundations of our society. the security, integrity and stability of the financial transfer system could be seriously jeopardised by the efforts of criminals and their associates to conceal the origin of the proceeds of criminal activities. particular attention should be paid to the fulfilment of the obligations set out in article 208 of the agreement on the functioning of the european union, which requires coherence in the development of corporate policy, in order to stem the growing trend of money laundering and activities increasingly moving from developed to developing countries. accordingly, the establishment of registers of beneficial ownership in the member states would give a significant boost to the fight against money laundering, terrorist financing, corruption, tax and other fraud and other illegal activities. all member states should establish financial units that are operational and independent and that analyse information in order to establish links between suspicious transactions.

madam president, i support the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use in the union, prepared by our colleague mrs sandrine bélier. in line with the objective of policy coherence for development set out in article 208 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, this regulation restores a fair balance between providers and users of genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with such resources, while contributing to the conservation of biological diversity and the sustainable use of its components in accordance with the objectives of the provisions of the convention on biological diversity. the european union should also act proactively to ensure that the objectives of the nagoya protocol on global multilateral profit-sharing mechanisms are achieved. the nagoya protocol aims to promote the sharing of genetic resources and traditional knowledge, in particular by promoting the sharing of genetic resources between developed countries and developing countries, and by promoting the sharing of genetic resources between developed countries and developing countries.
written. - the purpose of this regulation is to transpose the provisions of an international treaty known as the nagoya protocol into european union law. the protocol relates to genetic material and resources to which sovereign states claim rights and regulates their use. it also deals with the control of access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use. genetic resources and related traditional knowledge will be used subject to mutually agreed conditions between states. the parties shall cooperate in the development of the relevant international standards and standards, including those for the protection of the genetic resources of the parties. equal access and fair use will encourage biodiversity conservation and development, and i therefore support this report.

written. - i support this motion for a resolution by the european parliament with recommendations to the commission on the review of the european system of financial supervision (esfs). the european system of financial supervision consists of the three european supervisory authorities (esas) and the european systemic risk board (esrb), which were established by the regulations adopted in november 2010. the financial crisis has shown that risk management systems are inadequate and inefficient. such uneven and fragmented supervision of financial markets has contributed to financial instability and is part of the reason why there are shortcomings in the protection of consumers of financial services. the bodies within the european system of financial supervision are key actors in creating more stable and secure financial markets, and i therefore support stronger and better coordinated supervision at union level. at european union level, we must do everything we can to prevent the bad or inadequate financial management that ultimately affects the ordinary eu citizen the most. further adapting the 2010 measures, we will improve the functioning of the esfs through strengthened governance and authority roles and thus better equip financial control mechanisms and systems so that end-users of financial services are better protected.
written. - building on the lessons of the financial crisis and on the recommendations of the de larosière report, the european system of financial supervision (esfs) was established as a decentralised, multi-tier system of micro- and macro-prudential bodies. the supervisory system is currently undergoing major changes towards the introduction of the banking union. accordingly, the european parliament has expressed the need to organise european supervisory authorities (esas) with greater decision-making power and direct supervision, which it considers to be key to building stable financial markets. i hold that the proposal is unsatisfactory and accordingly i have not supported it. the commission is involved in esa's operations, where its involvement is not yet fully transparent, and its role in this area should be linked to the activities of the parliament and the council, without prejudice to the independence of esa. the current funding arrangements for the esa are also inflexible and create an administrative burden.

madam chairman, the protection of personal data is a major challenge today. citizens are the target of aggressive marketing campaigns targeted at them precisely on the basis of their personal data, which are used by marketing agencies beyond their wishes and their consent. this kind of data leakage is not typical of government agencies and institutions, but there is another fear among the public that we directly associate with the state. a large part of our citizens are wary of increased surveillance and suspicion of the unauthorized and unfounded use of the repressive apparatus and the secret services to limit their civil rights. however, i fear that such a proposal for a directive would make the work of the police and intelligence services considerably more difficult. the prohibition on the processing of personal data relating to ethnic and racial origin and religious affiliation will constitute a major constraint in the investigation and prosecution of war crimes and terrorist attacks, given that these elements in some cases constitute the main motive for such crimes.
mr president, we are having this debate while there are still some scandals that have been proven to have violated the right to privacy, as one of the fundamental rights of citizens of the union. it has been almost 20 years since the first data protection regulation was adopted. legislation needs to keep pace with the times and embrace the important technological developments of recent years, such as the development of social networks and the storage of data on external servers. i support proposals that the regulation will in future affect all entities in the european union, but also organisations outside the union that use citizens' personal data. member states should be encouraged to coordinate their legislative procedures in order to avoid any inconsistencies. i would particularly welcome the attention paid to the protection of children. i also stress the need to give users control over the amount of information they give out. it is necessary to prevent information seekers from requesting information which is not necessary for the performance of a service, in particular if they refuse to provide services without providing such information.

written. - turkey has been an associate member of the eu since 1964, when an agreement was signed between the eez and turkey (the ankara agreement). accession negotiations with turkey were officially opened on 3 october 2005, the same day as those with croatia. although from an economic point of view the advantages of such an approach are manifold and can be summarised in several terms: harmonisation of laws; new markets; new economic opportunities, and much greater investment and human potential, as well as for consolidation, peace and stability, and for the benefit of the entire continent. on the other hand, the disrespect for liberal democracy, which implies: discrimination against ethnic minorities (mainly against kurds), forced secularism and the significant role of the military in political life, the non-recognition of the state of cyprus show that turkey's progress is insignificant and many improvements are needed for a possible future approach. as i said, i abstained on this report.

madam president, honourable commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, the crisis has had a significant impact on the decline in competitiveness, the emergence of macroeconomic imbalances and excessive deficits in the member states. the problems facing some member countries are so severe that some economic analysts have begun to predict the collapse and end of the euro and the eurozone. however, with clearly defined objectives and well-defined activities, and thanks to the determination of the heads of state and the european commission to implement the necessary reforms, the negative trends have begun to change. europe is emerging from the crisis and the euro is becoming the most stable currency. one of the most important measures was the creation of the troika to help the most vulnerable member states financially and programmatically in the process of emerging from the crisis. a specific set of measures has been designed for each of the countries greece, cyprus, portugal and ireland as the causes of the crisis differed in each of the countries. the fact is that countries have implemented strong fiscal consolidation and that the short-term effects are not always in line with the europe 2020 objectives. so for example, lower wages mean lower competitiveness because the best ones go to other countries. reducing pensions and social benefits leads to an increase in poverty. reducing subsidies and incentives for entrepreneurs, if invested in the winners, is an obstacle to growth and development. however, the effect is still a reduction in debt and deficits, which, if accompanied by investment in development projects, opens the way in the long term for a return to higher wages, job creation and better social care, the main objectives of a competitive, innovative, development and social europe. the programme and the work of the troika have produced positive results. europe was not the source of the problem, but it was the source of the solution.

written. - the bailouts of the eurozone countries were carried out under strict conditions, checked and monitored by the so-called troika: the european commission, the european central bank and the international monetary fund. the troika was established as a back-up and emergency solution adopted under considerable time pressure due to the economic crisis, when ad hoc decisions to support countries experiencing extreme difficulties had to be taken in order to avoid a disorderly default and the spread of the crisis to other member states. since the troika's working methods and democratic accountability were called into question, parliament launched an inquiry which included a series of public hearings and delegations on the impact of the measures taken on the economy and people's lives. while i support certain points in the report, such as the various challenges the troika had to overcome in the crisis situation and the internal problem of the functioning of the organisation, the three institutions do not have equal responsibility and their decision-making is done at different levels of responsibility. i voted against because the creation of the european financial stability facility and the european stability mechanism outside the union's institutions represents a step backwards in the development of the union, to the detriment, above all, of parliament, the court of auditors and the court of justice of the european union.
written. - the report by mr cercas has shown in a credible way how damaging some of the policies of the troika in greece, ireland, portugal and cyprus have been. as can be seen from various parts of the report, aggressive austerity policies have consequently had a profound impact on the radical increase in unemployment, especially among young people. in addition, there are clear and worrying trends in increasing poverty and increasing social exclusion and the very marked marginalisation of vulnerable social groups. it is clear that the troika, in implementing the austerity programme, has enslaved itself to economic indicators, and this almost completely ignoring the fact that social indicators are an equally important element of the healthy development of our society. i cannot agree with economic policies that aim to correct mere statistics about economic growth, but which ultimately result in deepening the social gap between rich and poor, and reinforce deep social divisions whose conflict is economic in nature. the europe i see is a europe of equality and equal opportunities for all, with an emphasis on social sensitivity and concern for others. this is no time to use our politics to reinforce the divide between those who have much and those who have nothing. it's time to show solidarity more than ever. i am extremely pleased that mr cercas' report recognises this and i was therefore very happy to support it.

madam president, the economic interests of the european union are of paramount importance and it is necessary to establish appropriate instruments to enable the rights and the appropriate conditions to be achieved in the framework of international trade agreements. it is important to ensure flexibility, efficiency within the time limits and procedures defined by international trade agreements. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the format and content of the information to be provided to the european parliament and to the council. efficiency is also important in cases where essential raw materials are involved which may adversely affect european industrial and economic interests. it is of the utmost importance to harmonise the levels of protection of measures and concessions under international and trade agreements and to encourage third countries with which agreements are being established to introduce measures to improve trade. i support the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the exercise of the union's right to apply and enforce international trade rules, as this will greatly increase the union's ability to pursue its economic interests.
the european union currently lacks a horizontal legal framework for implementing its rights under the wto and other international trade agreements. at a time when third countries are introducing restrictive trade measures, appropriate instruments are needed to ensure the swift and effective enforcement of eu rights under international trade agreements and ultimately to convince our business partners to respect the rules as laid down in free trade agreements. the dispute settlement mechanisms under the wto and other regional or bilateral agreements seek to find a positive solution to all disputes between the eu and other signatories to those agreements. however, the union should suspend concessions or other obligations, in accordance with those dispute settlement rules, if other possibilities to seek a positive settlement of the dispute have proved unsuccessful. the measures taken by the union in such cases seek to encourage the third countries concerned to comply with the relevant international trade rules in order to restore a situation of mutual benefit. i believe that the mere existence of this regulation will dissuade our business partners from disregarding international trade rules, and the use of mechanisms will be only an exception.

written. - the financial crisis has highlighted the weaknesses of statutory audit, particularly with regard to public-interest entities (pii). the public-interest entities are credit institutions, insurance companies and other public-interest entities listed on a stock exchange and of high economic importance due to their size, number of employees and business activities. the purpose of this reform should, inter alia, be to remove barriers to entry in the audit market. the union audit market is controlled by four large audit firms, the so-called 'big four', with a market share of over 90%. such high concentration organises competition in the market and there are high barriers to entry for small and medium-sized audit firms, as well as limited choice in the audit market. unfortunately, i believe that this attempt to reform the commission will not strengthen confidence in the audit reports or provide security from the next crisis. auditing as it exists today does not provide sufficient insight into the annual accounts of public-interest entities and i insist on independent auditors who would provide clear, concrete and impartial reports.
written. - speaking of statutory audit, we must know how important it is that statutory auditors, audit firms or members of their business networks do not provide audited entities with any service other than statutory audit as this could jeopardise their independence. the auditors shall be appointed by the audit authority and shall be appointed by the audit authority. the auditors should be informed of the results of the audit procedure by means of an audit report. in order to increase the confidence of stakeholders in the audited entity's financial statements, it is important that the audit report is well reasoned and the content is extended by additional information. the audit authority shall be empowered to appoint the statutory auditor or the audit firm. the right of choice shall not be restricted by the conclusion of a contract with a third party which would limit the choice to specific auditors or audit firms. competent authorities shall be empowered to conduct investigations into statutory auditors and audit firms in the event of irregularities being detected and shall be able to cooperate with the professional bodies of auditors in all their activities. in view of all the above, i have a positive opinion of the report and have supported it.

written. - in order to increase the independence of statutory auditors and audit firms from the audit entity during the statutory audit of annual financial statements and consolidated financial statements, any natural or legal person having voting rights in the audit firm should be independent of the audited entity and should not participate in the decision-making process. in order to improve the transparency of the supervision of auditors, each member state should designate one body responsible for public oversight. the independence of that public oversight body from the audit profession is a basic prerequisite for the integrity, efficiency and proper functioning of public oversight. the public oversight bodies should therefore be managed by non-active auditors and member states should establish independent and transparent selection procedures. the burden on smes to audit their financial statements remains very high, but these reports do not provide sufficient insight into the situation of these companies and thus do not provide sufficient protection for investors. the commission should also be able to assess the impact of the proposed amendments on the financial statements of the companies concerned.

written. - the budget of the european environment agency for the financial year 2012 is eur 41 700 000, representing an increase of 1,25% compared to the 2011 budget. however, it is commendable and important to note that the share of union funds in the agency's budget has decreased by 0,23% compared to 2011. it is also commendable that the agency corrected all the comments concerning the 2011 discharge. the 2012 implementation rate is 99,19% and the payment appropriations execution rate is 89,41%. however, it is also important to highlight the comments that must be taken into account for the period to come. the agency has allocated grants under three programmes in 2012, and these grants represent 27% of the total operational costs, although the agency does not normally require beneficiaries to provide documentation to confirm the acceptability and accuracy of the costs shown. the agency's executive director's travel expenses for 2012 are also significantly higher than those of the executive directors of other agencies. it would therefore be desirable for the agency to further explain these costs to the discharge authority for 2012.
the european fisheries control agency is an independent executive body that cooperates with the european commission, the member states, regional advisory councils and third parties such as regional fisheries organisations. the missions of the said agency are numerous and they include coordinating the surveillance and inspection activities of the member states under the common fisheries policy, contributing to the joint research and development of new control and inspection bodies, organising the implementation of joint national control and inspection resources, etc. the agency is also of particular importance as it plays a major role in bringing member states closer together and ensuring better and more effective fisheries controls at community level through activities such as operational coordination, joint training of inspectors, implementation of harmonisation and exchange of knowledge and experience. according to the financial statements, the final budget of the european fisheries control agency for the financial year 2012 was eur 9 216 900, representing a reduction of 28,27% compared to 2011. i agree with parliament's decision to discharge the director-general of the european fisheries control agency in respect of the implementation of the agency's budget for the financial year 2012. i personally attach great importance to fisheries policy and welcome the agency's efficiency in carrying out all the tasks it fulfils.
the european fisheries control agency has a key role to play in the implementation and enforcement of the reform of the common fisheries policy (cfp). the requirements for the agency are becoming increasingly complex. large resources are needed to meet the growing need for monitoring, control and surveillance of fisheries activities. the agency's budgetary resources in 2012 showed a declining trend compared to the previous year, by 28,27%. the union's share in the agency's 2012 budget also decreased by 13,78%. i believe that in the years to come, we must ensure the maximum possible financial and human capacity in response to the constantly increasing need for monitoring of fishing activities. i come from the republic of croatia, one of the most maritime countries in the european union and europe in general. it is of vital importance for us that the agency for fisheries control works properly, because unfortunately, in recent years we have witnessed the illegal usurpation of croatian territorial waters. it is a common occurrence that italian vessels enter croatian territorial waters and fish there, disturbing the natural balance and causing immeasurable material damage to the republic of croatia. the once fish-rich eastern adriatic is now running out of fish. i therefore once again appeal to the european institutions to ensure that the european fisheries control agency is adequately resourced to enable it to carry out the task entrusted to it.
written. - the european food safety authority is an independent body with broad powers enabling it to monitor all stages of food production - from primary production, via animal feed safety, to the supply to the consumer. it also cooperates directly with the public, informing them of the issues it deals with. it is important to note that the agency may also initiate a risk assessment on its own initiative in relation to the current state of food safety and thus warn of possible hazards at the earliest stage. the agency also provides scientific advice on genetically modified food (gmos) and their impact on food safety. i agree with the european parliament in granting the executive director of the european food safety authority discharge in respect of the implementation of the agency's budget for the financial year 2012. the final budget for the financial year 2012 amounts to eur 78 279 000, representing an increase of 1,25% compared to the previous year.
the european food safety authority has broad powers to monitor all stages of food production, from primary production, via the safety of feed, to the supply of the consumer. technological advances open up the possibility of ever more sophisticated fraud that can seriously threaten human health and upset the balance of nature. the scientific findings of the agency are therefore of crucial importance, as only they can dismantle in time the lobbies in the food industry that seek only to maximise profits, without caring for the quality and correctness of the products placed on the market. the agency's staff is 70% employed in the scientific research sector, which means that the agency has recognised the importance of investing in scientific achievements in financial and human capacities in a timely manner. the budget of the european food safety authority increased by 1,25% in 2012 compared to 2011, with the union contributing 100% of that budget. given the complexity of the food industry controls, the agency's budget is expected to continue to grow in the coming years. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any information on the amount of the aid granted to the beneficiary. it is also commendable that the agency has taken corrective action to address the deficiencies noted in the 2011 comments.

member of the commission. - madam president, i would also like to thank the rapporteur, mr gualtieri, as well as the members of the high level working group, for their constructive approach to the revision of this transparency register. this register is an example of fruitful cooperation between parliament and the commission at a political but also a technical level. our cooperation is, after all, there to benefit european citizens, but it is equally for stakeholders engaged in lobbying, as well as for the institutions of the european union themselves. since its launch in june 2011, the register has shed much light on the brussels lobbying scene, answering questions about what interests are being pursued, by whom, and how much is invested in these efforts. today the website includes 6 500 entities of various natures and sizes – consultancies, ngos, think tanks, trade associations, law firms and also self-employed lobbyists. the register continues to grow every day, in my opinion demonstrating that we are on the right track. i would like to stress in this context that there is no charge for the regions. in many countries they have a legislative role to play and are therefore not covered by the register. regions can, however, register their representative offices in brussels if they so wish. the scheme can certainly be further improved. there are gaps in the representation of certain sectors and the quality of data varies. the website could be modernised and clearer guidelines could be provided for registrants. for instance, not all eu officials are aware of the register or use it. therefore we have not yet reached all relevant external stakeholders either. these are the challenges that the joint transparency register secretariat, supported by all those committed to transparency, should address. in 2017, at the time of the next review, we will again take stock of progress. the commission will shortly issue internal guidelines on the application of the foreseen incentives for registration. finally, let me be clear that the register is not the only transparency instrument implemented by the commission. other initiatives, promoted via the transparency portal, include for instance the regulation of public access to documents, the registers of experts’ groups and comitology, and information about recipients of eu funds. we look forward to further cooperation with parliament during the implementation of the revised interinstitutional agreement.

madam vice-president, the stability of the european financial sector is important for the future of the single market. but i believe that it should not take precedence over protecting the taxpayers whose money has been repeatedly stolen by irresponsible governments in an attempt to increase public spending to overcome the crisis. the banks were happy with this policy because it generated new debt and they supported the destructive and failed measures. delusional politicians have thus contributed to the destabilisation of the european financial sector. we are here today to protect this sector from collapse, but above all to protect our citizens and ordinary savers from new failed policies that would be funded out of their own pockets. i am therefore particularly pleased that under this proposal the funds for bank rescue will not come from the national budgets of the member states and i will therefore support it.
madam president, this is a step in the right direction. not a historic day. because it's not a historic day, is it, when we say that the bills have to be paid by those who made them? in fact, the financial and economic crisis is largely the result of the reckless and irresponsible behavior of banks, especially the expansionary credit policies that have resulted in banks printing non-existent money. the bill has come down on the taxpayers and everyone else who is not at fault. well, that should change now. at least the part that pays the bill for the underhandedness. what is at stake is that the banking system becomes or remains a state within a state. to answer to itself, and to use our money as a basis for printing its own, credit, virtual and in fact non-existent money. the next composition of this parliament will be responsible for ensuring that banks once again become a service rather than the centre of economic events in the european union and the member states.
mr. president, in times of crisis, citizens who cannot take care of themselves must be able to rely on the state. in the context of this debate, i would like to highlight two important directives on common rules for the internal market in electricity and natural gas which state that vulnerable customers are prohibited from switching off electricity and natural gas in times of crisis. i regret that croatia does not implement the aforementioned directives, although the current government adopted the energy law in line with the acquis of the european union in 2012, but unfortunately without implementing regulations. i would hereby call on the governments of the member states, with particular reference to croatia, to draw up an appropriate framework to enable these directives to be applied as early as next winter. i also believe that the funds needed to patch up over-ambitious government budgets should not be taken out of the pockets of citizens by introducing new or increasing existing charges for electricity, gas or other utilities.
mr. president, i take this proposal as positive, not just positive. i believe that today's decision by this european parliament is historic, because it contributes to the further integration of the internal market for banking services. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties. the financial and economic crisis has shown that the functioning of the internal market in this area has been compromised and that the risk of financial fragmentation has increased. interbank markets have become less liquid and cross-border banking activity is declining due to fear of expansion and lack of confidence in other national banking systems. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the establishment of a single resolution mechanism for the resolution of credit institutions and the resolution of credit institutions in the union. the commission and the board should also be subject to all other relevant provisions of union law, including binding regulatory and applicable technical standards.
mr president, the financial crisis that began seven years ago has shown that the european union still lacks the appropriate instruments to deal with the problem of failing credit institutions. both credit institutions themselves and individual member states should take responsibility and develop risk management programmes that should take into account the circumstances in which this crisis has arisen and the reasons for the failure. in this way we could prevent further possible crisis situations, possibly preventing another economic crisis in the future. the single supervisory authority should be established to rapidly and effectively remedy the damage to the institution or group so that the damage does not spread further, and in order to preserve the financial, economic, social stability of the country or countries in which the institution operates. in creating a single resolution mechanism, the adoption of this directive would establish credible rules that would sever the link between banks and governance structures.
written. - i am pleased that after three months of negotiations, an agreement has been reached on the single resolution mechanism regulations which should apply to all banks in all member states. the key to these negotiations was the position of parliament expressed at the january plenary session and the commitment to create an effective, independent and predictable mechanism with adequate financial resources. parliament succeeded in further adapting key items such as the decision-making process, the single resolution fund and the architecture of the single resolution mechanism. the agreement between the stakeholders also made a breakthrough in dealing with unsound credit institutions and investment firms that the european central bank will now be able to close down if they are deemed too weak to survive. the single resolution fund will have €55 billion available for eight years, two years shorter than the plan proposed by the council. each country participating in the banking union will have its own national drawer in the rescue fund, while each year the national share will decrease and the common share of the fund will increase simultaneously. although the council has not allowed the amendment of the intergovernmental agreement, i ultimately support the draft of this regulation which is in many ways an improvement on its original proposal.

he is seeking the presidency of the council. - i know . madam president, ladies and gentlemen, you understand how important it is for the greek presidency of the council, which attaches particular importance to cultural heritage, to take part in this debate on behalf of the council. the directive on the return of cultural objects unlawfully removed from the territory of a member state is an important tool in tackling the illicit trafficking of cultural objects, which is now one of the most widespread forms of organised crime. the 1993 directive did not, however, meet expectations. this is due to the short deadlines, the eligibility criteria, the level of compensation and the lack of administrative cooperation. the text we have now agreed with the european parliament is a significant improvement. there are four main improvements: first, the annex containing the categories of cultural goods eligible for refund is deleted. from now on, any cultural object considered by a member state to be part of its national treasures shall be returned because of its particular artistic, historical or archaeological value. secondly, the extension of the individual time limits gives the national authorities in charge of the return procedure more time to do their job. national authorities now have six months instead of two months to check whether an object located in another member state is a 'cultural object' within the meaning of the directive. the time for initiating the return procedure before the competent court has also been extended from one to three years. thirdly, with the introduction of the internal market information system, the competent national authorities are equipped with a tool that improves administrative cooperation and the exchange of information. we hope that this new system will speed up cooperation and reduce costs. finally, the fourth and perhaps most important feature of the directive as it is now formulated is the fact that the payment of compensation is subject to the obligation of the holder to prove that he or she has exercised due diligence. a presumption is therefore established. the directive introduces uniform rules in all member states, shifting the burden of proof to the holder. this regulation is crucial to preventing and combating the illicit trafficking of cultural goods, as it will create a level playing field for all those involved in the art market. i am glad that we have achieved our objective of reaching an agreement in less than a year. we can be very pleased with the result. i should like to thank the hardworking rapporteur, mrs vergiat, and the chairman of the committee on culture, mrs doris pack, for their constructive contribution to the negotiating process. i would like to thank commissioner tajani and the european commission. finally, i would like to point out the interest shown by the shadow rapporteurs in this matter and thank them of course for their time and contribution. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am well aware of what it means for a country to feel culturally disadvantaged when it loses important national treasures. speaking not on behalf of the council but as vice-president and minister for foreign affairs of the greek government, i can only refer, on the occasion of this debate, to the major issue which is the mutilated monument of the parthenon the mutilated major monument of western civilization. parliament has already adopted a written declaration in 1999 that the return of the parthenon sculptures to greece would be a key opportunity to promote the common european cultural heritage, and this should be noted in connection with the updating and improvement of the directive on the return of cultural objects. it is a monument whose architectural elements are fragmented, while the new acropolis museum, which is now hosting working dinners for all the ministers and other officials visiting athens as part of the greek presidency, is our main argument for the need to reunite the monument and return the parthenon sculptures. i should also like to mention the damage to the cultural heritage of the republic of cyprus following the military invasion of 1974, which affected the archaeological and other cultural treasures of the island in a very characteristic way. the european parliament, by adopting this directive, is sending a message that for our europe the cultural dimension, that is to say the dimension of europe's cultural heritage and common historical consciousness, is always very important. thank you, sir.
vice-president of the commission. - madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, today's vote represents a step forward for the protection of cultural heritage in the internal market and, looking back, as the rapporteur has also pointed out, we cannot say that the 1993 directive on the return of cultural property has been particularly effective. the return of goods between member states has been rare in the european union and has not been able to counteract the losses and negative effects of illicit trafficking in cultural goods. the commission wanted to remedy this ineffectiveness by a major reform of the directive. the new directive will greatly facilitate the return of cultural property identified as national treasures of artistic, historical or archaeological value between member states, thus contributing to the conservation of such heritage. this will enable the member states to recover all national treasures which have been illegally removed from their territory since 1 january 1993 and the citizens of these member states will no longer be deprived of proof of their identity and their history. the main new features include: first, the extension of the scope of the directive to all cultural objects classified or defined as national heritage; second, the time limit for submitting a refund application is reduced to three years. third, in order to obtain compensation, the burden of proof of due diligence for the acquisition of the cultural object is on the possessor. finally, let me remind you that the prevention and combating of illicit trafficking is a task for all of us and must be exercised by all means at our disposal. this directive therefore forms part of the more ambitious perspective of protecting national heritage. i also think it is particularly positive that this house has recognised the importance of the proposal and has committed itself to adopting it so quickly. finally, i would like to thank parliament and in particular the rapporteur responsible, mrs vergiat, and the shadow rapporteurs for their efforts and commitment during the negotiations. on this occasion too, on the eve of the european elections, we have succeeded in defending europe's cultural heritage and in striking a blow at the criminal gangs who organise the trafficking of art objects, damaging national heritage which is also europe's heritage.
on behalf of the s&d club, i congratulate the rapporteur on having summarised most of the problems faced by member states in the recovery of cultural property. despite numerous safeguards, after drug and arms trafficking, the trafficking of cultural goods remains one of the most widespread forms of illicit trade. within the union, 40 000 works of art are smuggled into the union each year. first of all, we need a common definition of national cultural heritage to ensure a set of rules that is equal for all. because as long as the definition differs between member states, so will the practice. as the newest member of the union, croatia is extremely keen to extend the application of the directive to cases of alienation of cultural property committed before 1993. while the european union was abolishing market barriers, which was one of the reasons for adopting the first directive, croatia had to defend its national borders. during that period, 22,829 museum objects and 3,097 cultural objects were looted. a good part of it was restored by 2008, but since then, a little over 100 objects have been restored. the ministers of culture of croatia and serbia signed a protocol on the return of cultural property by the end of 2013, but this was not achieved and the implementation of the protocol continues. as this is an example of an open question between a full member and a candidate country negotiating membership, i welcome this directive - it can help to resolve this issue as well. i think the return of cultural property should be part of the negotiating package like any other adjustment.
madam president, i would like to start by congratulating the rapporteur on her excellent work. in particular, i believe that changes to the existing directive were necessary to make it more efficient and to make it work. i welcome the deletion of the annex specifying which categories of cultural goods meet the conditions for return and i fully agree that it is up to the member states themselves to define which cultural goods they consider to be their national treasures. the problem of returning illegally removed cultural property particularly affects the country i come from. the situation is somewhat different - cultural goods are not smuggled out of croatia, but simply looted. during the war, in the 90s, many cultural assets were looted and taken to serbia. the directive on the return of cultural objects unlawfully removed from the territory of the member states of the european union will regulate the return of such objects from 1993. however, many of the illicitly removed cultural goods from croatia were removed before 1993, i.e. 1991. i believe that can be regulated on the basis of the protocol signed by croatia and serbia a year ago. as a candidate country, serbia should speed up the return process, as only just over half of the items seized have been returned so far, and i believe that this directive should become part of the acquis and an obligation for all potential eu members.

written. - intrastat is a system for collecting information and producing statistics on the trade in goods between the countries of the european union. it started work on 1 january 1993, replacing customs declarations as the source of intra-eu trade statistics. statistics are an important factor in the development of european internal market policy and market analysis. the definition of statistical value needs to be clarified and harmonised to allow for better comparability of intra-eu and extra-eu trade statistics. uniform definitions are necessary for proper and unhindered cross-border trade and are particularly important as a prerequisite for different national authorities to be able to interpret in a harmonised manner the rules affecting the cross-border activities of business operators. the exchange of information through national authorities should be free of charge for member states and union institutions or agencies. following the recent discovery of breaches of the protection of data of union citizens and member states, there is a need to strengthen the security of the transmission of sensitive statistical data. the national authorities receiving confidential data must treat the data as confidential and use them only for statistical purposes.

written. - central securities depositories (csds) are private financial institutions that are essential in contributing to and maintaining the efficiency of the post-trade infrastructure. the effectiveness of those institutions guarantees market participants that a securities transaction will be executed in an orderly and timely manner. in addition, despite the growth of cross-border settlement, settlement markets in the union are still fragmented and cross-border settlement is more expensive due to different national rules governing the settlement and activities of csds and limited competition between csds. this fragmentation is disruptive and creates additional risks and costs for cross-border settlement. the proper functioning of the internal market requires the creation of an integrated securities settlement market, without distinction between national and cross-border transactions in securities. for that reason, i am satisfied with the outcome of the agreement on this subject. the most important features achieved are: the obligation to settle all transactions within 2 days after the trade (t+2), penalties for non-execution, the reporting of all settlement details to competent authorities by the csd, the reduction of the regulatory burden on smes markets and the requirement for csds to store on an aggregated basis securities lending and redemption data which would then be available to competent authorities.

written. - the brussels i regulation is the basis of judicial cooperation in the eu in the field of civil law. it covers a wide range of issues, covering not only binding but also substantive legal relationships. it determines the jurisdiction for the settlement of cross-border disputes and ensures the unimpeded recognition and enforcement of judgments given in another member state. the regulation is generally considered to be a success, but shortcomings have been identified that now need to be addressed. the proposal aims to remove the remaining obstacles to the free movement of judgments in accordance with the principle of mutual recognition. judicial cooperation and trust between member states is at a high level and the conditions have been created for the creation of a simpler and cheaper system for the circulation of judgments and the elimination of existing formalities between member states. the amendments relating to the unified patent court are intended to establish the international jurisdiction of that court. the court of justice should be able to rule on disputes involving third-country defendants on the basis of a subsidiary rule of jurisdiction in a specific case where a union claimant brings proceedings before a common court against a third-country defendant in respect of an infringement of a european patent which has caused damage inside and outside the eu.
written. - the agreement on a single patent court will avoid multiple proceedings that could be brought before 28 different national courts. the joint tribunal should be able to adjudicate disputes involving third-country defendants on the basis of a subsidiary rule of jurisdiction in a specific case where a union claimant brings proceedings before the joint tribunal against a third-country defendant in respect of an infringement of a european patent which has caused damage inside and outside the union. the joint court should exercise such subsidiary jurisdiction where the property belonging to the defendant is situated in one or more member states which are parties to the agreement establishing a joint court and the dispute in question is sufficiently connected with one or more of those member states because, for example, the claimant is domiciled there or because evidence relating to that dispute is located there. in establishing its jurisdiction on that basis, the common court should take into account the value of the property in question, which should not be insignificant and which should allow at least partial enforcement of the judgment in the member states party to the agreement establishing the common court. i believe that this will create a system of uniform patent protection throughout the european union.
written. - the single patent system is extremely important for the european union. until now, we have seen a complicated system of patent protection that has been costly and time-consuming, and has resulted in a low number of patents being filed in the european union. since innovation is what drives society, it is essential to enable inventors and businesses to establish cheaper, simpler and more effective patent protection. the unified patent court shall have exclusive jurisdiction in matters relating to the validity of the european patent. this will eliminate the risk of multiple litigation in different countries over the same patent and the risk of different decisions on the same patent. it is also necessary to regulate disputes with third-country defendants in disputes concerning at least one member state. i consider it essential that the single european patent court regulation should enter into force as soon as possible and therefore support this report.
